utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning. May I begin in the usual manner, by calling for the appearances, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Di Fazio, I appear for the Prosecution this morning, together with my colleague and case manager in this case, Mr. Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Slobodan Cvijetic appearing for Stanisic Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, Eric Tully, and Ms. Katarina Danicic, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, may we have the witness returned to the stand, please. MR. DI FAZIO: As the witness comes in, perhaps I can let the usher -- court staff know that I'll be using 65 ter 78 to start with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. I would remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 78, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, on Friday we were discussing -- I was asking you about the events in April of 1992 concerning the division -- or rather, the creation of Serb police stations, and this document touches upon that issue. As you can see, it's dated 10th of April, 1992, and it goes to the chief of the CSB department and all chiefs. And attention to various chiefs of a number of municipalities. Sanski Most is not mentioned there, but it is later. And if you look at -- MR. DI FAZIO: And Your Honours, please, this is the first paragraph on the 2nd page, and it appears on the second page of the document, the words beginning "tim povodom" Could you just have a look at that paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, that document describes a meeting of the SR BH collegium. And it talks about an enlarged CSB advisory counsel being held in Banja Luka CSB on the 7th of April where the security situation was analysed. And then in the next paragraph it goes on to say that in addition to members of the CSB collegium, the chiefs of various municipalities, Banja Luka, Bosanska Gradiska, and so on, including Sanski Most attended this meeting. Did you attend any meeting on the 7th of April, that is the meeting that this document refers to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember quite clearly a meeting held on the 6th of April, but I can't believe that was even on the 7th in Banja Luka, I just can't believe that, as it says here. I really don't remember bing there on the 7th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The document then goes on to state that a number of conclusions had been adopted unanimously. And that various public security stations are to come under the auspices, under the control, under CSB Banja Luka. And number 11 -- MR. DI FAZIO: Which, if Your Honours please, is on the third page of the document. And in the B/C/S it's on the third page in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can see the Serb municipality of Sanski Most is to become part of that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio, could you take a look on the page second, line 18 and 19. There is no answer here so maybe you can clarify that. Because maybe there was some problem with the transcript. Your question started with "could you just have a look ..." and then there is no answer. He answers something, and then there is another question of yours. It's line 18 and 19. MR. DI FAZIO: There's some problem with the transcript, but it's been rectified, I believe, I'm told by the recorder. Yes. I'll just continue. I think if there is any problem, we can return to it. Does Your Honour -- my question I think was did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I was there on the 6th of April, and I'm almost certain that I wasn't there on the 7th. I know that I was there for one day only, and I'm sure I wasn't on the 7th there. I would have remembered something if I were there. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I understand your position. Is there -- I hope that suits Mr. Pantelic's concerns, takes care of Mr. Pantelic's concerns. Yes. Anyway, the document then goes on to say that the Banja Luka services centre is going to be organised in various ways, and it's going to be joined by various public security stations. And number 11 on the list is Serbian municipality of Sanski Most. Do you have any knowledge of that procedure being made known to you, that being known to you sometime in early April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the Municipal Assembly of Sanski Most there was an extensive debate about attaching Sanski Most to the Autonomous Region of Krajina, but I know that it was never adopted by the Assembly. So it seems to me that this is impossible. As far as I remember, until 10th of April the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most hadn't been declared or proclaimed. Therefore, I don't know who did this. It didn't happen either in this joint parliament, or that any number of the Serbian deputies got together and adopted such a decision. I really don't remember any such thing taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The Paragraph 3 of the English which is contained on page 3 and which appears at -- also page 3 of the B/C/S says that employees have to sign the solemn declaration - that's the interpretation I have - the solemn declaration identical to the solemn declaration from the previous law. And there's a dead-line of 15th of April, 1992. Was that dead-line -- any such dead-line, any such dead-line, made known to you by Mr. Zupljanin at any time or by any document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Last Friday on several occasions I answered this question pursuant to Mr. Zupljanin's order not to take anything in Sanski Most, so it was not up to me to do anything. But rather, this gentleman was afraid that someone else might try to do something and he wanted me to know that this shouldn't happen. That is why he told me about Kljuc, Bosanski Novi, and Prijedor, that we should stay together even for a year if necessary without doing anything, regardless of what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, there was no need for me to abide by what is written here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you look now at paragraph 17. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, that's the page 5 of the English, paragraph 17, and it appears on the very last page of the B/C/S version of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 17 says that all authorised employees who don't sign the solemn declaration and aren't going to return to the service have to hand in their weapons. Were you tasked with any such -- did you receive any such instruction?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't have received any such instruction. On the 6th of April meeting when Mr. Zupljanin distributed these berets and these copies of solemn declaration, he said something to the effect that these solemn declarations, wherever that was to be put into practice -- but he didn't think that should have been done the police, it was up to Municipal Assemblies to declare themselves a Serbian municipality. And then within that context, as we went along the police should get in line with this kind of commitment of a municipality. So he -- something about these solemn declaration for the employees who wished to remain, they should sign them. I don't remember his saying that anyone who refuses to sign should be laid off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. But my question is more confined. My question is simply this: Paragraph 17 says that authorised employees - that's police - who don't sign the solemn declaration have to hand in their weapons. Now, did you receive any instruction that policemen who didn't sign the solemn declaration had to hand in their weapons at Sanski Most police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally didn't receive any instruction. On this 6th of April joint meeting, I heard that and everybody else who was present. But Mr. Zupljanin said that you in Sanski Most should refrain from that because it doesn't apply to you. Therefore, I had no obligation in that respect. It is true that I took these berets and solemn declaration, put them into the boot of my car and locked it there, and that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. We've heard that evidence and no problem in understanding that. That's okay. It's just, what I'm asking about is the handing in of weapons by those police officers who don't sign the solemn declaration. That's all. It's very focused. Not berets, not oaths, but the handing in of weapons. Now, did you receive any instruction that those who did not sign -- those policemen who didn't sign had to hand in their guns and weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving that, and I never did that. When we split up, all the Muslims and Croats left the station with all their small weapons and rifles. Nobody asked them to do anything of the sort. So the very act of separation on the 17th of April ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you would agree, wouldn't you, that the effect of that, if it were -- if it existed and if it were to be carried out would be to disarm Muslim and Croat police?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, leading question. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'll withdraw it. If Your Honours please, I seek to tender the document into evidence. And without going into the arguments that we've spoken about in recent days, if you're not with me, then I would ask at least that it be marked for identification, but my primary application is to put it into evidence as a full exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, as I appreciate the witness's answers, it seems to me that it should be marked for identification because he's distanced himself from the contents of this document in large part. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes, of course. It does of course contain considerably relevant material, and it's signed -- or not physically, doesn't have a handwritten signature, but it is a document authored on the face of it by one of the accused, Mr. Zupljanin. And it deals with all of the arrangements that were leading up to the division of the police and the creation of the Serb police in mid-April, at least, in Sanski Most. And the witness has spoken about all of those matters including instructions and -- that he received from Mr. Zupljanin. Plus that, some of the procedures mentioned in the document marry up with some of his evidence. So for that reason and given the fact that it's highly relevant and probative value, I would seek to tender it, but that's as far as I can take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, can I ask you, do you recall having received this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So it was sent by Mr. Zupljanin, as I understand it, to all the chiefs of the SJBs, but it never reached you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I don't recall this kind of document. I don't remember it at all. And particularly, I wasn't at -- because I wasn't at the meeting when this was decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 7th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The document is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P355, marked for identification, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one last question on the document. The type face, the way the document looks, the setting out of the document with headings, the way the distribution list is written, and generally the format of the document, does that accord with police documents that were being produced in 1992, the sort of documents you saw day-to-day basis in carrying out your duties?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may relieve you of your anxiety, Mr. Di Fazio, the Chamber bearing in mind the distinction between a document which is admissible as opposed to admitted, the Chamber has no difficulty what order in terms of the admissibility of this document. So I think I understand why you're asking that question, but it probably isn't necessary. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Very well. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, I've finished with the document. I want to ask you now about another topic altogether, the arrival of the 6th Krajina Brigade. You touched upon this topic last Friday. You said that the army arrived in Sanski Most, and I think it was on or about the day of your meeting on the 6th of April. Do I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the night between the 6th and 7th of April, during the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And very briefly, how -- what sort of strength was this army unit at? How many men was it at -- did it contain?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a complete 6th Krajina Brigade, made up of all the Serbian soldiers who responded to the call-up, including a number of Croats and Muslims. Many Muslims didn't respond to the call-up, therefore that was a sort of rump brigade, particularly due to the reason to a large number of Muslim and Croats not having responded to it. As far as I remember, it's numbered about 3.000 troops, but I don't know the exact number. I never saw them in one place all together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you. 3.000. Thanks. That's what I wanted to know. And did you meet with the commander of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met up with him as soon as they arrived. I think he came to have coffee with me the next morning. He went to see me and the commander and tell us that he was there, and when I went to Palanka on an errand, I also went there to see where the command was based. I think it was in Palanka. That's where the brigade was. I found Basara there as well, we had a coffee together, we had a conversation, and then I returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Basara was the commander, was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the conversation about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation in general. I don't remember any details. I came to greet him. He offered me a cup of coffee. We had one together, and then it was me, actually, who sent a letter to him and the brigade, the 6th Brigade should return to Sanski Most. And on that occasion when we met up again he told me, "I am here to prevent a conflict in Sanski Most." And we talked about other things, of course, but I remember him repeating that that's why he was there with his brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he there also to assist police in maintaining order and ensuring that conflict did not break out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not see each other again until - what was it? - the 17th of April when he came at 8.30 in the morning. Before that we did not have any other contacts. On the 17th, though, he came early in the morning to my office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question. Was he there also to assist police in maintaining order and ensuring that conflict did not break out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. If he had received an assignment to come and prevent inter-ethnic conflict, then that would have implied cooperation between the army and the police, each acting within their own purview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And in fact you had written to him in mid-March, seeking the return of the army to Sanski Most. That's what you testified on Friday. What did you explain in your letter in mid-March that you wanted the army to do when they returned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, seeing how inter-ethnic tensions grew worse almost every day and since Mr. Zupljanin had told me before that nothing should be done in Sanski Most as in other municipalities, I, realising that inter-ethnic conflict may break out, got the idea that I should invite the brigade to come and help out. Nobody, I suppose, would be so willing to incite a conflict if the brigade was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you report to Mr. Zupljanin, your regional chief, that you had taken this step of inviting army formations, groups -- brigade, I should say, into your municipality?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember whether I informed him or not. If I had not, I certainly should have, but I don't remember whether I did. I should have -- I must have sent at least a letter to him saying that the 6th Krajina Brigade was in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree with me that that is -- that sort of information, the request and invitation to bring in armed formations into the municipality is precisely the sort of thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Leading again. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You must have anticipated that objection, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll move on. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the meeting where you actually met up with Mr. Basara and you were discussing matters upon his -- when he first arrived, did you and he discuss specifically how the army might help the police, what exactly they might do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At our first meeting, Colonel Basara dropped by just briefly. We just had a coffee together and he said, "I'm here to prevent conflict in Sanski Most," and that's -- that was all. We did not talk about it anymore. It was quite enough for me that he was just there. I was quite reassured and certain that nothing was going to happen in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The army was based -- the 6th Krajina Brigade was based at a place called -- was it Lusci Palanka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where the command was, and the brigade probably had its own wartime deployment in the surrounding villages. You couldn't see them. They were located and based on the surrounding hills and camps --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... only the commander was in Lusci Palanka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how far away from the police station is Lusci Palanka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 25 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work out any procedures that you and Basara would follow in the event that you had to call upon him for assistance in maintaining law and order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember talking or planning at all. In fact, I remember we didn't. He said, "I'm here to prevent inter-ethnic conflict if it arises," and for me that was a guarantee that nothing would happen. If anything had happened in the meantime, of course we would have met again and agreed what to do, each in our own jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you now about -- move on past the 6th of April. In the days immediately following the 6th of April and leading up to the 13th of April, did you hear anything more about the activities of the SOS in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was completely quiet in Sanski Most, at least those few days between the arrival of the brigade until the 14th. It was absolutely quiet in Sanski Most, as far as I remember. There were no incidents or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mr. Rasula in between the 6th and the 13th of April?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Zupljanin again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was the 6th, I can't remember -- I don't think -- I don't think I went to Banja Luka between the 6th and the 13th. Maybe we talked on the phone, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. What about on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th I met up with Mr. Zupljanin in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did that come about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of April, within the police station there was some sort of panic. I was informed that the SOS had asked Rasula for an urgent meeting of the Executive Board of the SDS, where they would come with an ultimatum to take over the police. And that afternoon, since I usually did not attend meetings -- and it was quite strange to me that Rasula was informed about it rather than Vlado Vrkes, who was the president of the SDS. But as soon as I was informed of that meeting, I knew why he was inviting me to come. And then I replied that the next morning I was going to the centre to see Mr. Zupljanin on official business. He said, "Fine," and he knew probably that I was going to see Mr. Zupljanin because of the information that was circulating that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Who told you? Who informed you that the SOS was going to take over the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got that information from the police, and everyone talked about it that day with quite a lot of anxiety and fear. I saw in people's eyes that they were frightened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not an easy thing to hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've testified -- so you had police intelligence that the SOS were going to take over the police, and you've told us that the police thought there were about seven or eight people, and you knew one of the leaders or some of the leaders. Did you take steps to -- in those circumstances to go out and arrest them on that very day, put them in prison and charge them with something?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I believed, and we in the police believed, that there were about seven or eight of them because we never saw them as a group. But we never had any verified information about it. Those were rumours circulating around town and at the police, that it was the SOS. We did not know much about them. We knew that there were about seven or eight people who met frequently. We had no verified official reports, and we did not dare make any estimates or plans, precisely because we didn't know how many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thanks for that. Did you consider at least going out and talking to them, sending some police officers out to talk to the seven or eight SOS members about this new intelligence you had, perhaps make some inquiries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said last Friday that those seven or eight we knew about had no criminal records, they did not have even a misdemeanour record. They were not violating law or public order. Even when these crimes of bombing happened, when explosive devices were set, we couldn't catch anyone. And they acted quite normally, like any other citizen. I didn't see any reason to go and interview them. What would I tell any one of them?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you might have told them something to the effect that the police suspected them of throwing bombs and that they've received information to the effect that they are going to take over the police station, is there any truth in this? Did you consider asking them that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't talk to them because we had no such reports before the 13th of April. There were no reports that they might attack. They went around town and acted quite normally, like the most peaceful of citizens. We had no reason to believe that they might be responsible for any incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had had such information, then we could have invited them for an interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Thanks. Well, one thing you did do is you went off and spoke to Mr. Zupljanin the following day; do I understand your evidence correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went to see him precisely because I needed to tell him what the SOS was planning and to ask him for advice, what we were supposed to do next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what advice did you receive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first he tried to persuade me that I should talk to them, impress upon them my authority to dissuade them from whatever they might be planning, and I said, "What authority?" I had done my best to catch them at whatever they were doing, and if I failed, then what possible authority would I have in their eyes? On the contrary, any such action might get me killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just explain to the Trial Chamber why the issue of authority and sufficient authority arose as an issue, because they were -- they were the most peaceful of citizens. Why was it -- why did authority arise as an issue between you and Mr. Zupljanin when discussing what to do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zupljanin tried to talk me into meeting with them and act as someone who has authority. I said I have no authority as far as they're concerned because I didn't know any of them personally. I knew them only by sight. I had no arguments. And if they were really those SOS members, as we suspected, then there's no reason to believe that I would have any authority. That's one. And second, after what happened in Banja Luka, what the SOS did, and if we know that all these SOS men used to be members of the 6th Krajina Brigade and the 6th Krajina Brigade was already in Sanski Most - and we now know that the 6th Krajina Brigade had been in various theatres of war before - it's quite clear that most of them had been elsewhere, in battle-fields, and they were in Sanski Most only on leave. But only now when the whole brigade was in Sanski Most we were able to see how many of them were actually there, in the brigade. And we realised that it might be the biggest mistake possible to clash with them. And then the third thing is if the army was already there, then the army should take care of it; why me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that the SOS membership -- members of the SOS in Sanski Most were also members of the 6th Krajina Brigade? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all of them were soldiers of the 6th Krajina Brigade, very few of them were in the TO, the Territorial Defence. Most of them had already been in various battle-fields in Croatia for the past ten months. And if they were involved in such crimes, that means that they were the sort of people who dared to -- we can only suppose what would happen if we risked a big clash with them. People already talked around town, saying that they were some sort of paramilitary organisation. People in town actually knew more than we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, when you went and had the meeting with Mr. Zupljanin following the news that the SOS is going to take over the police station, did you know or have any intelligence or information that the SOS membership was -- basically SOS members were also members of the 6th Krajina Brigade? Because your evidence up till now has been that there were seven or eight lads as far as you were concerned. So when did it become clear to you that you weren't dealing with seven or eight local lads, but a group that existed within the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any knowledge, any reports, about the way SOS was organised. They acted as the SOS, but they never held out themselves to be the SOS. It's the people who labelled them SOS. None of us in the police had ever received any information from them directly that they were the SOS. They did not identify themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was only on the 14th when they asked for a meeting with the SDS did they identify themselves as the SOS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just try and answer the next few questions very briefly, if you would. At the 14th of April meeting with Mr. Zupljanin, did you receive any instruction from Mr. Zupljanin to disarm the SOS in Sanski Most, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer this with a yes or no. When Mr. Zupljanin realised I don't actually dare to do what he was suggesting - he was quite aware of it, that I didn't dare to - and when after all the talking when he realised I didn't even dare go back to Sanski Most if he made me do that, he said, "I know these people, they're very dangerous. If they really had set their mind to it, they're going to do it. Go back, Majkic, and try to settle things down in a quiet way, without shooting. And at least try to have this thing handled peacefully."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just explain to the Trial Chamber just one part of your previous answer. You said this: "When Mr. Zupljanin realised that I don't actually dare to do what he was suggesting ..." You went on to say other things. Now, what -- what in a nutshell, in brief, clearly, was Mr. Zupljanin suggesting that you do? What did he want you to do in the face of this situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to quote him. He said, "Majkic, go, and if there's any way to do it without a shoot-out, do it. If it can't happen without a shoot-out, then try to take care of both," he probably meant Croats and Muslims, "and keep them safe. If you are not able to save everyone, then at least try to minimise the casualties." That's approximately what he said. I'm trying to quote him. And finally he said, "God help us."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. But -- and I'll return to my other questions then. He gave you no specific instruction to disarm the SOS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How on earth were we supposed to disarm the SOS, a paramilitary unit, when the 6th Krajina Brigade was already there? They had to have the entire security situation under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And finally it wasn't even our job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you or he suggest that you enlist the aid of the 6th Krajina Brigade to make sure that these SOS members don't take over the police station or attack this public building in the centre of town, enlist their help?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 14th at 4.00 p.m. at that meeting, just after I had met with Mr. Zupljanin in the centre and came to that other meeting, there were members of the Executive Board of the Serbian Democratic Party, three members of the SOS, and there was the intelligence officer of the 6th Krajina Brigade. He was there, he was present. I don't think that the SOS had invited him or the SDS had invited him. Colonel Basara must have sent this intelligence officer, which means that Colonel Basara knew what was going on. The intelligence officer from the brigade was at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you about the meeting, we'll get into that. But all I'm asking you is a very simple question: On the 14th when you were sitting in the office with Mr. Zupljanin, did you and he before the meeting, before the meeting, before you went back to Sanski Most, there in Banja Luka face-to-face with Mr. Zupljanin, did you and he discuss the possibility of enlisting the aid of the 6th Krajina Brigade to stop this take-over of the police station? Was that raised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already told you the whole story about what he tried to get me to do. When he realised I didn't have the guts, he said, "I know these people. They're very dangerous. If they had set their mind to it, they're going to do it. So go try and handle it peacefully. If it's not possible to handle it peacefully, if there's a shoot-out, try to keep everyone safe. If that is not possible, then try to minimise the casualties." That was our whole conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's turn to the meeting that you've already alluded to. This is a meeting on the 14th, and after the meeting with Mr. Zupljanin - and I don't think there was any dispute that it was at the Orthodox church - about what time did the meeting start? Just give us the time, just the time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't in an Orthodox church, it was in the parish residence, which is next to the Orthodox church. Before and now, this is a school for priests. That's one thing. Secondly, the meeting was convened for 1600 hours, and I arrived there at 1730 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And were any members of the SOS present?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said earlier, the SDS executive committee, three SOS members, and the brigade intelligence officer were at the meeting when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Who were the SOS members?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were Dusan Saovic, a.k.a. Njunja; Dusan Modrinic, a.k.a. Medeni; and the third one had the nickname Cirija. I don't know his name, not even to this date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you arrived late. Did you learn anything that had happened in the time prior to your arrival at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I couldn't have learned of that. At the time I arrived I saw this ultimatum that was put forth by the SOS and I had the information about that from the day before, and I realised that they were discussing this ultimatum because I see that the people from the SDS Executive Board were very worried. I saw that on their faces. I assume that they were even more afraid of the SOS than the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they accepted this initiative, or rather, when they discussed it, since Mr. Rasula knew that I had seen Zupljanin, he asked me what Zupljanin had to say. Although I never told him why I met with Mr. Zupljanin, I responded by saying that Mr. Zupljanin wanted this to be done in a peaceful way if possible. I didn't say anything other than that, and that is when some of them said that a Crisis Staff needs to be set up and this Njunja, as a kind of SOS leader, said, "We have a proposal for the Crisis Staff as well." So not only did they come with a proposal for the ultimatum, they also came with a proposal for the Crisis Staff and then he read this proposal. Once the Crisis Staff was set up, the Executive Board of the SDA [as interpreted] decided to start negotiations with the SDS -- SDA and the HDZ about a peaceful split, and this is what happened in the days afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. There's just one aspect of your answer that I'd like you to clarify for the Trial Chamber. Rasula asks you what happened between you and Zupljanin. You responded by saying that Mr. Zupljanin wanted this to be done in a peaceful way. What? What was to be done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that these men came with an ultimatum, they had to accept this ultimatum, but they were nevertheless waiting for me to come and see what news I had. And when I said that Mr. Zupljanin --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... asked for this to be done by -- in peaceful way if possible --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, my question is simple. There's no need -- it's very simple. It's only this, it's only this. You said that Mr. Zupljanin wanted this to be done in a peaceful way if possible. What did he want to be done in a peaceful way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Zupljanin wanted them to do it in a peaceful way, the thing that they had planned. I was never thinking about how and what. When they said that they intended to take over the public security station - and despite all our discussions and thinking - he did ask me to have it done in a peaceful way. How? The only peaceful way is through negotiations. What I said was sufficient for the SDS to decide to enter the negotiations with the SDA and HDZ about division of power and peaceful separation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. We'll get on to the SDS and SDA later, but just focus on the meeting now at the parish building. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, in fact, perhaps what I'll do is just ask that the witness be shown P60.13, which is the diary that we've looked at earlier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I want to ask you about entries that appear at page 13 of the English, and that in the B/C/S are exactly 16 pages into the document, so it's 16 pages in. It's a handwritten document. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours just give me a moment. I've got to make sure that I've got the right portion of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: On the B/C/S I think it carries the date 26 November in print at the top. I think that's the correct part in the B/C/S, which I think -- page 32. I'm told it's page 32.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you can see it there -- I hope you can. I'm referring to an entry dated the 14th of April, 1992, and heading above that says: "Course of action in taking over power and establishing the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it might be --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, now I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Got it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Course of action of taking over power ..." --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... "and establishing Serbian municipality of Sanski Most."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. I apologise for that delay. Right. Now I want to ask you about that entry. It says -- it refers to a radical mode of attaining objectives being undertaken. Do you know what reference that might be to -- to what that might be referring?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read this. If you can read it out for me, then I'll try to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. It says: "Following extensive and continuous inter-party agreements based on the principles, based on electorally agreed on regulations, and on basis of electoral results dictated by political events in Yugoslavia and Bosnia, a radical mode of attaining objectives has been undertaken ..." Have you any idea what that radical -- what those objectives might be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't answer that. You should ask the author of this. I really don't know what kind of answer I can give you. I have no answer at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can we go down to point 4, and I think we can see it there on the B/C/S in front of our screens. Point 4 in the B/C/S. It says: "The Crisis Staff consisting of the following members shall be in charge of all actions ..." Thank you. All right. Now, you can see all of the names, some of them you've mentioned. And you're mentioned there. Were you on the crisis --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Simple question: Were you on the Crisis Staff? Can you account for that entry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when the SOS suggested -- rather, Njunja suggested and read their proposal about establishing a Crisis Staff, this proposal, apart from Rasula and Vrkes and myself, it included also Dr. Nikolic. But Rasula and Vrkes were not in the SOS proposal. So when they read their proposal, there were eight of us excluding Vrkes and Rasula. After that I immediately got up and said that I -- and offered some explanation why I wouldn't like to be on it. The same happened with Dr. Nikolic. He gave some kind of explanation, and it was immediately accepted by the SOS. After that, Vlado Vrkes, as the SDS president, got up and proposed that he and Rasula should become part of the Crisis Staff based on their posts and positions. The SOS accepted that, and then the executive committee of the SDS party took a decision to adopt this proposal. That is how the Crisis Staff was established, without me, and the last one, not Nikolic Zvonko, but his name was actually Nikolic Viko. Probably Mr. Rasula had some instructions from the top, that is to say from Mr. Karadzic, about who should be on the Crisis Staff and that should have included the chief of police. I didn't know that, and that is why I proposed that I should be excused. I think that Rasula knew that, and that is why he put me on the list. That could probably be found in some SDS records. That's the only explanation of how my name got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for explaining that. You mentioned that Vlado Vrkes and Boro -- sorry, not you. The document mentioned Vlado Vrkes and Boro Savanovic are there to conduct negotiations with the SDA from 10.00 to 1.30. Do you know what negotiations they were tasked with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was Vrkes and Savanovic. I think that Rasula, Savanovic, and a third member - I'm not quite sure - were tasked with this assignment. But it was Savanovic and the other one who met with the SDA and HDZ. The very following day, they decided to split in a peaceful way because they had been informed about what happened on our side the day before, and I think the dead-line was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is kindly asked to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The dead-line was the 17th of April, noon. And I think that after that they started dividing the villages and everything else. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Negotiations are mentioned there to last until about half past 1.00 in the afternoon, and then it describes a process that is to start at 2.00 in the afternoon. And that is measures taken in relation to the building and public -- police employees. It says that entrances and stairwells and so on shall be secured by reliable men. The 6th Krajina Brigade is going to lend a hand by providing a platoon of reservists. Full alert of the 6th Krajina Brigade. And the building is to be secured from within by the national defence secretariat, and the Crisis Staff is to have a liaison man, namely Braco Papric. Do you recall all of those plans being discussed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't attend these negotiations at all. The Wednesday 15 -- 14th and Thursday the 15th, the commander and I went to the municipal building where these negotiations were taking place to see how they progressed. The second or the first day we arrived, we were told that there was an agreement but there was some outstanding matters. So I don't know what they actually agreed, and I don't know if the 6th Krajina Brigade was mentioned in these negotiations at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. I'm not talking about the next day or negotiations. We'll get on to that in due course, and you can tell us about that. I'm just talking about the meeting there in the parish house next to the Orthodox church. This document says at that meeting, that various measures were planned. Negotiations lasting until 1.30, and then at 2.00 in the afternoon a session of the public service employees begins at 2.00 and various matters are to be taken care of, entrances and stairwells and the warehouse secured, et cetera. You can see them written there. Were those measures discussed at the meeting, while you were present anyway?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to tell me exactly what meeting you're referring to, what is written here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meeting on the 14th are -- when you came back, having met Mr. Zupljanin earlier that day, and you went to the parish house where the SOS were and the 6th Krajina intelligence guy was and SDS Executive Board, that meeting.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember - and I remember very well - when I came there an usher asked me what had Zupljanin said, and I responded as I did. The Crisis Staff was set up on the spot and the SDS and its executive committee decided to establish a commission to conduct negotiations, and that is where the meeting ended. Whether this -- these things happened in the one and a half hours that it last before I arrived, I don't know. When I arrived -- and this second part of the meeting that I attended ended very quickly with all these decisions taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, do you propose to take a break shortly? Because this might be a good moment to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Are you saying that your next line is going to take longer than five minutes? MR. DI FAZIO: No, but I can continue if you wish. I'm not quite sure what time you would like to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 10.25 is the usual. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. All right. Can we go to the English page 15 of the document. That's an entry dated after the 17th of April. I'm not entirely sure where it is in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I'll read it out to you and -- anyway, I'll read it out to you. It's an entry saying: "Responsibilities and implementation of agreed actions from 17 April 1992. "Carry out separation of the police forces by 1200 hours. Dragan Majkic in charge." Were you tasked with any particular responsibility relating to separation of police forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th and the 16th, negotiations took place. At about 2.00 or 2.30 on the 16th when the commander -- I arrived at the building and asked them if they had made any agreements, they told us, yes, but there was some unresolved things. Then we went home. In the evening at around 2300 hours, after I'd gone to bed, the telephone rang and somebody called me from the Crisis Staff to come to a house that was a couple of hundred metres from the police station and that I had been summoned by the Crisis Staff. I went there, and I saw that all members of the Crisis Staff were there. I didn't want to interrupt what they were discussing. I just sat down and listened to what they were talking about. They were planning to attack the police building. I suddenly interrupted them and said, "Excuse me, what is this that you are planning?" I think that it was Vrkes who chaired this meeting, judging by the way where he was sitting. He said that, "We have to attack the police building." I asked him, "How can you do that? Because at any moment I always have 20 people outside and 20 people, fully armed people, inside the building." And he said, "We have to." And I said, "Why?" He said, "The negotiations had failed. Once we agreed everything else, the only outstanding, unresolved issue, was the police building. We offered them to move to the Sip building and that we retain the present building. However, they refused that, but they insist of having the police building for them, one floor should belong to them, and the other to us. And since this failed, I said we have to attack." On that Thursday I already had the information that the Muslim and Croat policemen who already had collected all their personal stuff and took them home were saying openly because -- saying openly that they were not coming back because everybody knew that the division was to take place the following day. I told Vrkes, "Please don't attack. There's no need for that. I will agree with the commander for a split in order to avoid this." He was very happy that I suggested that because he, himself, was completely frightened. He was pallid, just like everybody else. I looked at them while they were discussing this, but I just saw that they were frozen with fear. They were just relieved to hear what I wanted to suggest. They immediately accepted my proposal not to launch an attack at 5.00 a.m. the next morning and to allow me to agree with the police to split in a peaceful way, and that is where this meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What precisely was terrifying the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not an easy thing to enter into a conflict and attack police at that. When I asked them who's going to attack with them they said, "SOS." I told them I had 20 people fully armed outside the building and 20 fully armed people inside the building. How do you think you can do that? But he said and his voice was shivering, he said, "We must do that." And I said that, "Let me settle this with the commander." And Vrkes told Majkic, "If you manage to pull this through, I will be in debt to you for the rest of my life. And it's on my -- I'll take you to a restaurant, my treat."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So presumably the Crisis Staff was looking for any solution to avoid an armed attack and jumped at your offer to negotiate; I understand correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was really something out of the heaven. They were relieved immediately and they were not in such a bad mood as they had been when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps one last question before I leave this topic, and then I imagine the break. Presumably the Crisis Staff, then, and not the SOS, was in a position to decide if and when an attack would take place, because they delayed it once you made your offer; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one from the SOS at that meeting. That was the Crisis Staff. I'm talking about the meeting in the evening, the Crisis Staff and no one else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. But from what you've told us, it's clear, isn't it, that the SOS -- sorry, the S -- the Crisis Staff was the body calling the shots on when the attack should take place, from what you've said?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection. It's -- first of all, I think it's time for a break, and then after that my learned friend can rephrase the question because it's two-fold, multi-fold, it's loaded. It's unclear, the question. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I was trying to clarify evidence that occurred earlier -- that came earlier this morning concerning the influence of the SOS on this body. And now we've had some evidence from the witness to the effect that the Crisis Staff is deciding on times for the attack, an attack in which the SOS is to participate. Now, it's those two pieces of evidence that I'm trying to get a further understanding of. That's why I asked that question. I want to know who it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could return to this after the break because it struck me that the objection would not have been as Mr. Pantelic articulated it, but that it was having regard to the testimony of the witness up to this point. It's the type -- it's really a conclusion that you're asking the witness to give. But as I said, we can think about it during the break. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, just before the witness comes in, there's just one matter I very briefly want to raise with you and that's this: I seek your leave or permission to use another document today that I haven't included on my list. And I'm mindful of the comments on Friday and -- so I'm not doing this in a cavalier fashion. I want to use 65 ter 603. It's a Crisis Staff document from the 24th of April. It -- I thought it had been on my original list, but I've checked and unfortunately it wasn't. I've spoken to the Defence and I gather that there's no particular objection to that. I would intend to use it briefly and spend a minute or two on it at the end of my examination-in-chief and I can make hard copies and have them brought here into court to lessen any inconvenience that might occur to you because of my failure to put it on the list. So that's what I'd like to do if there is no -- if the Trial Chamber's content with that, then that's what I'll do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No objection from Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And it was on the 65 ter list? MR. DI FAZIO: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, yes, it's one of our 65 ter exhibits, but I hadn't included it on my list of documents I intended to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's just the late notice that they are going to use, so we don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For Zupljanin, also we don't have any objection. MR. DI FAZIO: And I'm not going to dwell on the document at all, but would Your Honours like hard copies? I can get hard copies brought to you, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I did promise to return to Mr. Pantelic's objection when we resumed, and it seems to me, as I said at the break, that having regard to what the witness has testified to, isn't the question asking him for a conclusion which is properly the province of the Chamber, unless of course your question is in the context of some action that he subsequently took consequent upon his own personal conclusions of the events of the 14th of April? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, yes, I take Your Honour's point. There will be further evidence about the SOS, but none in the sense of it, as far as I'm aware, dictating what this particular witness did. So I don't need to pursue the question any further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. We were talking about Thursday night, the 16th of April, and you talked about this meeting. Was -- just final clarification on the meeting. Was every member of the Crisis Staff present from what you can recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think they were all there. To the best of my recollection, they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And I might have asked you this before but I just want to be absolutely clear, there were no SOS members present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the following day, that's the 17th, did you go to the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that morning I came to work at the usual time, 7.30 or 7.00 perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you discuss anything with Enver Burnic, the man who was your commander of police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to work, first I looked through the reports to see what had happened the previous 24 hours, reports that the duty officer put on my desk, and then I invited him to talk. When he came, I informed him about everything and I told him, "Commander, just so that we don't provide any provocation for a conflict, as some people seem to expect, I give you approval that you, Croat and Muslim policemen, take leave until Monday morning to force the SDS to accept what Mr. Vrkes had told me about, that proposal that Sip building be given to them as a location for their bodies. I will put pressure on the SDS to clean out the building until Monday morning, the beginning of working hours, so that you can resume work normally on Monday there. And in the event that the SDS fails to vacate the Sip building, then on Monday you come here to work normally, business as usual." The commander liked the proposal. He accepted it willingly. He seemed happy. And then suddenly he jumped from the chair and said, "I have to call the SDA to ask them." I told him, "Enver, don't," because I thought the SDA would not accept it. It was just a hunch. So I told him, "Don't do that, please. Let's do as we agreed. I hope it's for the best." But then he told me, "I really have to call the SDA." He went to his office, he called, came back, and said, "The SDA ordered me not to leave this building." I told him very frankly, "I told you not to call them because now you have to do as they say." So we went on talking and then at 8.30 Colonel Basara came into the office, and as soon as he sat down he said, "I came here to prevent an inter-ethnic conflict. I will not have any inter-ethnic conflict here in town." So we went on talking and we were happy that he joined our effort to prevent the conflict, and for a full three hours he kept sitting in my office and we kept talking until 11.30. Around 11.00, the duty officer from downstairs called me and there was a Muslim officer on duty that day. That policeman asked me whether to go home now or to wait for -- to wait until 12.00. And I told him, "Whatever you decide. It's up to you." I don't actually know what they decided. At that time there was only Enver Burnic and that policeman in the duty room. They were the only Muslims there. Enver left the police building around 11.30, and by that time the SOS were already deployed around the police building. I don't know how he could have failed to see them as he was leaving the police building. He must have seen them and he should have intervened. Did he ever wonder what they were doing there? I can't answer for him of course. But then the commander and I stayed in my office and kept talking, and then at about five to 12.00 two policemen came to my office and told us, "The police downstairs are demanding a meeting. The employees are demanding a meeting." I looked at him uncomprehendingly and said, "Which employees?" And he said, "Everyone, Serbs, Muslims, Croats." It seemed quite illogical to me if at 11.00 there were only the commander and that other Muslim in the duty room. What employees? But anyway we went down and it was true, everyone was in the hall. So I addressed these people and told them all the same things that I told the commander. I put forward my proposal, and everyone accepted it gladly, just as the commander had, they all agreed. But for some reason, they did not dare to leave the building; why, I don't know. So we were stuck. People began telling jokes. I know the commander always had his passport in his breast pocket, and as soon as his banter started, he took it out and said, "I'm always ready to run." At exactly 3.00, Rasula came through the door and pointed at his watch, looking at me. And he tells me, "Majkic, the separation was planned for 3.00." And I said, "We were just talking about that." And he says, "What is there to talk about? You were supposed to be separated by noon. All those who want to stay in this building and work had to sign this declaration. Those who won't have to leave." Then Zikrija Bahtic got up --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter does not understand this. Could the witness slow down and repeat. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down. Slow down. The interpreters can't hear you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Rasula said that a separation had been agreed, then this Zikrija Bahtic got up and said, "Is that so, President?" And Rasula said, "That's what we agreed." And at that, everyone got to their feet and left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see a gentleman named Tomo Delic that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as they were gone, Delic who was alone or with someone, I think he was with someone, came into the room and said, "Don't even think of any -- putting up any opposition. We'll put the Serbian flag on the police building." And I told him, half jokingly, "You are the only one who dare do such a thing." And that's what they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Was a member of the executive board, SDS Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a member of the Executive Board because he was always present at those meetings. I can't remember all 25 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I think he was a member of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you do anything in respect of the berets and the declaration, the oaths, or declarations, or whatever they were concerning -- that you'd been given?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Croat and Muslim policemen left, we remained on our own. I went to my office and everyone followed me. I thought at the moment that the separation had taken place, and all those berets that were still in the boot in my car, I had one policeman fetch them together with the solemn declarations. And that policeman brought them. And then we proceeded to sign these solemn declarations, and everyone who signed got this beret with insignia on it --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... two Croats were left at that time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. How did you know to distribute the declarations and the berets at that point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Di Fazio, I wouldn't like to interfere, but I believe the witness wanted to say something else, and he was cut in the middle of a sentence. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry. I didn't mean to cut him off, but I am conscious of time. And -- but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll make sure that the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: -- fulfils his answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I cut you off. You were talking about the solemn declarations and everyone who signed the beret -- and everybody who signed got a beret with insignia. Did you want to say anything more about that particular topic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say this: As I was to distribute these berets, the policemen said, "Vlado Lopar," one of the two Croats who remained, "wants to be the first to sign." And I said, "No problem." So this Vlado Lopar signed the solemn declaration and received a beret, and then they all followed, one by one. All those who remained in the building, in other words, signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber what it was that triggered you at that point to go and get the berets and the declarations.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that moment I was aware that the separation had happened. There was an inter-party agreement between SDS on one hand and the HDZ and the SDA on the other hand. They had all agreed on this dead-line, 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whichever way, it did happen. Mr. Rasula was practically in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm not -- there is an intervention in transcript. 39, line 13, I believe the witness gave the -- "they had all agreed on this dead-line," and he gave the date as well and the time. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the date of the dead-line for the separation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you now, Witness, we're going to move to another topic, to keep your answers as brief as you can. We've got limited time, and we need to try and wrap this up. How far away -- just give us a short answer. How far away is the municipality building from the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Direct your mind to Saturday, 18 April 1992. Did anything happen in relation to that building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, Friday, the 17th -- in fact, in the small hours on the Saturday after, around 1.00 a.m., Muslim and Croat policemen headed by the HDZ and SDA respectively went into the municipal building and took it over. They made their base there and said it was their building now, and that's where they would locate their bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that day, the Saturday, did you go to the building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That morning the police called me up and informed me of what had happened. I had just come to work and I was waiting -- in fact, I don't know what I was waiting for, but these people from the Crisis Staff also came. And they were going to the municipal building to negotiate with those HDZ and SDA people. And that Saturday, once or twice I stopped by this large office where many policemen were sitting. I sat down with them, had a drink, we talked, and we were waiting for the outcome of these negotiations. By that time the Crisis Staff was leading the whole thing and the HDZ or -- and the SDA. In fact, I'm not sure whether the SDS was negotiating with the Croats and Muslims or the Crisis Staff. In any case, I was sitting there in the room of the policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did these negotiations continue over the Saturday and into the Sunday? Just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saturday and Sunday the negotiations lasted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn your mind now to the events of Sunday night, Sunday, 19 of April, please. On that night did you see Mr. Rasula?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 8.00, Mr. Rasula came to my office and Boro Savanovic from the Crisis Staff and Mirko Vrucinic, the three of them came to my office. Mr. Rasula sat down in my chair, and there was a discussion about these negotiations, that they had talked, that they had failed to agree. I don't remember the details. Anyway, that's what the discussion was about. It lasted until about 9.00 p.m., and then at 9.00 p.m. Rasula took the -- picked up the receiver and said, "Now I'm going to give them an ultimatum that they have to leave the building until" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the hour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Until 10.00." The SDA president took the call and Rasula told him, "If you don't vacate the building by 10.00, we will take the building over." And he hung up. Around 10.00 Mirko Vrucinic went to the municipal building to see what was going on. At 20 to 10.00 the telephone rang. Mr. Rasula picked up the phone and somebody informed him that SDA and HDZ members had left the building, but the police remained inside. Hearing that conversation, I intervened with Mr. Rasula immediately and warned him that the police was probably not informed of the ultimatum; they were not aware of it. I picked up the phone. I called the police room and Commander Burnic answered. I asked him, "Enver, do you know about the ultimatum?" He said, "What ultimatum?" I told him, "At 10.00 the building will be attacked. Collect your men and leave the building." He said, "Fine," and hung up. At ten to 10.00 the telephone rang again. Rasula answered and somebody told him that the commander and another three men left the building, got into one police car that they had taken, and two other men who had driven their own cars to work also left. The others were still in the building. At 10.00, when shooting started, those who were still inside the building were probably frightened because the SOS was already on the other side of the building. They did not dare escape that way, so they jumped through the window and ran in the opposite direction. That way at 10.00 there was no one left in the building, just the guard. There was not much shooting. I don't think any bullets actually hit the building. Most of the shooting was in the air. The guard was crouching in a corner, terrified. Then Rasula got another call around 10.30 and somebody told him, "President, here I am, I'm sitting in your office." So it was all over. I went home around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And was a Zolja rocket-propelled grenade weapon used?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, one Zolja was heard. An SOS man did not want to shoot at the building. He was shooting at a tree next to the entrance. He did that on purpose. He didn't want to shoot at the building because they probably knew there was no one inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So essentially there was -- I'll withdraw that question. MR. DI FAZIO: I want to show the witness a document, please, it's 65 ter 597.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we can see it's a Crisis Staff document. It's dated 20 April 1992, and it's gone to the chief of Public Security Service in Banja Luka and a Serbian newspaper agency. Who was the chief of Public Security Service Banja Luka at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. And it's an announcement, and it says - and I'm looking at the third paragraph - that: "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most is of the opinion that force had to be used during the liberation of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly building from armed formations of the extreme faction of the SDA leadership. Long and exhausting talks simply failed to bear fruit." Now, do you recall any such announcement being made by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this being proclaimed, but it probably was. It could have been in the newspapers, on the radio, but I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I seek to tender the document into evidence, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P356, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 602.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to get through this document as swiftly as we can because we're -- got time constraints. So I'd just like to ask you to answer a few questions about this document and be as brief as you can. It's dated 22nd of April, 1992, and it's got -- it's apparently signed by the Crisis Staff. And I think if we look at the bottom of the B/C/S you can see a stamp there, Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sanski Most Municipal Board. Now, the document, firstly -- some of the names here you've already spoken about, and we know some of their names, Ned Rasula, Vrucinic, Vrkes, Savanovic. There's a man there named Mile Gutes, and paragraph 3 concerns his assignment at Sanski Most Serbian radio station. All I want to know is very simple thing, I don't want a big long explanation, all I want to know is do you know of a gentleman actually named Mile Gutes, and was he in some way connected with radio in Sanski Most? That's all I want to know, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was the husband of one of our employees who worked on ID cards, and at that time I had heard that he was enlisted to become the director of the radio station because he was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if he was in that position, I think he didn't stay there for long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. One other name that we may not have mentioned to the Trial Chamber thus far is in paragraph 5. Vrucinic is mentioned again and then Mladen Lukic. Who was Mladen Lukic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a member of the Crisis Staff, a lawyer by profession. He worked for the utility company in charge of general affairs there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Go to paragraph 6. "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most adopts a conclusion that the Serbian defence forces are to be placed at the disposal of the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence and engaged as a special unit ..." Is that a reference to the SOS, the Serbian defence forces?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says clearly Serbian defence forces, therefore SOS -- but it's not clear to me how come that all of a sudden a paramilitary unit is attached to the Territorial Defence because all of them were fighters with the 6th Krajina Brigade. I don't know how this decision was taken. Maybe Colonel Basara wanted to get rid of them, but I find this decision rather odd. But yes, at that time they were attached to the Serbian Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So on the face of it, on the face of it, this document would indicate that the Crisis Staff was able to exert control over the SOS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably they decided to put them under their control, because before that they were not under the control, and with decision they were put under the control and they ceased to be paramilitary unit, if they were one, and to become part of regular forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that document into evidence. In support of my application, he's made -- the witness has given esoteric information that tends to bolster the authenticity of the document.
