The evidence relating to Gutes, his some somewhat particular occupation. It's got a stamp on it as well. And the characters are all men that he has discussed and spoken about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P357, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move along swiftly. The following day, Monday, that's Monday, the 20th of April, did you go to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know whether I went to Banja Luka on the second or the third day to see Mr. Zupljanin, but I doubt it was on the second day. So it would be a few days after these events that I went to see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Whenever it was, whether it was the -- Monday or the second or third day, what did you discuss with him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply went there to inform him about everything that had taken place and how it all went. I know that he was very glad that it was finished in a peaceful way. He was very satisfied that it went peacefully without shooting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was satisfied with what in particular, the taking over of the police station and the municipality building or just one or both?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what he was satisfied with, but as I say, that it went without any shooting except for a few shots fired around the municipality building. He was happy to see that no one was injured or hurt. He was extremely happy that there were no casualties incurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he give you any instructions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him giving me any instructions. I simply informed him that the entire territory of the municipality was covered by the active-duty police force; that the situation was very quiet and there were no problems; and that I had erected certain check-points, were only meant to check vehicles not citizens. Therefore, the police work as such went as usual, only with reinforced numbers. And all through to May I don't recall any incident or any problem arising or any complaints coming from the citizens to me. So everything was under control and people went to work normally. I'm not sure only about that first Monday after the event, but the day after, when we saw that the situation was back to normal, everybody came to work, the employees, the supervisors, and everything else. It all lasted until the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you now about the period of time between Monday, the 20th -- yes, Monday, the 20th, and Thursday, the 30th of April, 1992, that period of time. You told us already that you started to carry out your police work. In that time, did a gentleman named Simo Drljaca visit the police in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it happened five or six days later or three or four days later. Anyway, the Crisis Staff called me to attend a meeting in that period. When I arrived there, I saw representatives from Prijedor, one of them was Simo Drljaca. I don't remember who the other one was. And Vinko Kondic from Kljuc, the chief from Kljuc, had come accompanied by somebody from the SDS. So there were about four or five new faces on the Crisis Staff. The meeting --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you. Could you just explain to the Trial Chamber what occupation and position Simo Drljaca and Vinko Kondic held.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vinko Kondic was the chief of the Kljuc SJB, and Simo Drljaca was in Prijedor, he was a lawyer not working for the police. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And what did -- okay, please, go on and explain to the Trial Chamber what these men were here for -- were there for, and in particular what Drljaca was there for.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came there simply to see the model of how we took over power, in order to apply the same model in their municipality. So after this lengthy explanation, they went away without comprehending at all how we did it, and I noticed they were really not happy with that, how was it possible for them not to do what we did, because they didn't understand a thing. And that is why later on in Prijedor during the take over of power, a lot of policemen got killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they weren't very pleased with your model of taking over and they went on -- they had their own, as events later bore out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not displeased with our model. They only couldn't understand how we managed to reach this outcome. It was impossible for them to do that, not in a million years. They probably wanted to apply the same model, having seen that there were no casualties, and they wanted to do it the same way; but it was impossible under their circumstances, in their situation. That's as much as I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Boro Savanovic is a relative of yours, is he not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And we're still focusing on those ten days, 20 to 30 of April. During that period of time did he give you any information about your -- security of your position as police chief?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of those ten or so days, I had no idea that the Crisis Staff was meeting, except for the meeting attended by people from Prijedor and Kljuc. However, Boro Savanovic and Nemanja Tripkovic would come to see me every evening and try to persuade me to resign. However, I didn't want to accept that. I had some arguments with them, some light-hearted arguments, I have to say, and then on the evening of the 29th, when they came again to try to persuade me, and I again told them that I didn't want to withdraw, Boro Savanovic, a relative of mine, told me, "Man, if you don't resign, they're going to kill you." Then I realised how serious it was, and then on the following day when they called me to the Crisis Staff I told them that I was willing to resign.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown 65 ter 2366. Yes, 2366.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So another Crisis Staff document. This one is indeed dated 29 April, and -- I only want to direct your attention to two paragraphs in particular. First, paragraph 5. And it says: "In connection with appointing the chief of the public security station and the functioning of the Sanski Most STO, Nedeljko Rasula and Nedjo Anicic are instructed to visit Banja Luka." Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And paragraph 4 above says: "That a sharp statement to be issued on punishment in connection with the disarming of paramilitary formations in Sanski Most ..." and that your relative Savanovic was in charge of this. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I wasn't at that meeting. I know nothing about these decisions. I didn't even know before the 30th of April that the Crisis Staff was meeting occasionally. Therefore, I cannot comment on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: And can we just scroll down on the B/C/S version and perhaps look to the next page of the B/C/S version and the page after that, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document has got a stamp there. Do you recognise that stamp?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that resembles a stamp of the Serbian Democratic Party, at least the coat of arms that I see in the middle. Around that, it's a bit blurred. I cannot read it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I seek to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection, because -- I turn to Serbian. [Interpretation] The witness did not identify a single portion of this document, nor did he admit to knowing anything about these meeting -- about these decisions. And he also knew nothing about the meetings taking place, therefore there is no nexus between what is said in the document and the testimony given by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, the document is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P358, marked for identification, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can the witness be shown 65 ter 1846, 1846. All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. This document is ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment, please. Thanks. While we're waiting for any problems to be sorted out in relation to that document, I can move on to 606, 65 ter 606. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, on the face of it a Crisis Staff document. This one's dated 30th of April, conclusions of the Crisis Staff. And the one that concerns you is paragraph 2. And it says that: "The Crisis Staff ... hereby appoints and certifies that Mirko Vrucinic is going to start his job as acting chief of the public security station ... from the 1st of May ... at 9.00 ..." and that they undertake to find a position for you. Does that correspond with what, in fact, happened? Did, in fact, Vrucinic start as acting chief of public security station on the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Crisis Staff meeting that I was invited to attend was precisely for the purpose of informing me that Vrucinic was to become chief, and I was offered the position of the chief for national defence. However, I told them I didn't want to leave the police force. And then during all these wrangling and during my explaining to them that this was not the way to dismiss them, they didn't want to listen to reason. They just wanted to dismiss me. I at least asked them to send a telegram to Zupljanin so that he knows, and then they refused to do that. They even refused to call him by phone. They just said, "Please get up and Mirko will sit in your chair." They offered me different positions, but I refused them. So there was a kind of stalemate. They simply didn't know what to do with me. I, myself, knew, but I didn't want to accept that. So we just sat there staring at each other. When I realised that they didn't know what to do, I told them to tell me to take a five-day annual leave, during which time Vrucinic would find an appropriate position within the public security station that was corresponding to my qualifications. Finally they accepted that, and I decided to resign and I left the meeting. Therefore, I only stayed there while this item was on the agenda, and after it has finished I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I seek to tender that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. I suppose inasmuch as he was present for part of this, he is saying, that this is slightly a different category from the -- MR. DI FAZIO: It is, at least to that extent, and it has got -- his evidence accords with paragraph 2 from that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P359, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: And could I just quickly show the witness 2741, 65 ter 2741.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. It's really the first page that I'm interested in, first and last page. So on this page, the first page of this document, which is entitled: "Job specification and employment overview in Sanski Most SJB on 13 May 1992," the first page shows that Mirko Vrucinic is chief from the 4th of May, 1992. Again, without reading out anything just cast your eye down the page, look at those names of those police there, typists, finance, maintenance people, were they all police working in Sanski Most at the time? We know about Vrucinic. I'm talking about the others.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all the employees working at the police station at the time, at least those on this page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. And just go to the very last page, it's the last page on both documents, English and B/C/S. Perhaps the second-to-the -- perhaps the second-to-last page of the B/C/S. Yes, I think that's better. It says -- well, first of all, do you recognise those names as employees of the SJB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we don't need to dwell on this. I can simply lead you through this. On the last page your name appears, it says unassigned and 4th of May, 1992, previously chief, all of that is true. You were in the police and you were previously the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P360. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now turn your mind to the period of time after all of these events that you've been talking about, after you were dismissed from your position as police chief. Firstly, do you know of a place in Sanski Most called Betonirka garages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Betonirka garages, that was actually company making concrete products. It was close to the public security station, not more than 50 metres. Those were the garages belonging to this company. I suppose you are referring to them, they were close to the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks. And do you know of a place called Krings Hall in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. That was a company established before the war. It was a German company and it was in operation before the war. That's why it was called Krings Hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know of a sports hall in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's a town sports hall in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the months after the end of April, were prisoners taken there, to those places?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours. Both my and Mr. Pantelic's LiveNotes are not working, therefore we are not in a position to follow both the transcript and the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand it's a technical problem which is affecting everyone, and they're trying to sort it out now. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, I misunderstood. I didn't realise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sports hall, Krings Hall, and Betonirka. Were those places used to detain prisoners in the months after your dismissal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not going to work. I only went once a week. As for the Betonirka building, I never went there. I did hear that there were prisoners there. As for the Krings Hall, on the way towards Lusci Palanka, when I was passing by in my car, I could see people inside the hall. I saw a few reservists and soldiers standing guard. I went to the sports hall once to intercede for one young man to get him out of there. I went on that occasion with Nemanja Tripkovic, who was kind of in charge of that hall, humanitarian sort of thing. So when I went to get that young man out, I saw the place. I don't know anything about Betonirka; I never went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. What was the ethnicity of the people in those three locations? The prisoners I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats -- I mean probably. You know, who else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And you said that you interceded on one occasion for a young man. What was the young man's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you successful in getting him out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was released a few days later I think -- in fact, I don't think, I know. But, look, those people were from Mahala. There was a sort of skirmish on the 4th. People left the Mahala, there was no one there anymore. People dispersed around town, everybody found accommodation somewhere, and then the army rounded them up around town, put them into the hall, and then they were transported via Bosanska Krupa towards Cazin and Bihac. So I interceded that time for a young man from Mahala. His mother was friends with my wife --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and that was the connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Do you have any recollection who was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again, the witness was cut in the middle of his answer, Your Honours. I believe he should be -- I understand the concerns my friend is having with the time, but I still believe that the witness should be allowed to answer in full. It's -- MR. DI FAZIO: No, I understand --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It struck me that the witness was interrupted because he was going off into peripheral information which isn't particularly helpful. MR. DI FAZIO: That's precisely what I was doing. I didn't want to get into the relationship between the mother and the boy, and so on. It just wasn't germane to any of these issues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were prisoners also taken to the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the police station, statements were taken from them -- I mean, as far as I know. I would come once a week only for about a half an hour or an hour. Statements were taken from these people, and if nobody had a -- someone had a record, then they were kept and detained in those facilities. And if you did not have any record, then they were released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What ethnicity were these people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats. I don't know if there were any Serbs among them. That's what I heard from the people in criminal investigations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any problem with accommodating these prisoners at the police station?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a remand facility adjoining the building of the police station, and that's where I heard all the leading people from the SDA and the HDZ and even some policemen were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. 57 -- page 57, line 3 and 4, it's entered into the transcript that somebody who had a record then they were kept and detained in those facilities. I don't think that the witness had said exactly that. Maybe my friend can re-address. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier, just a moment ago, that -- in answer to the question of whether prisoners were taken to the police station, that you would go there about once a week for an hour and a half, statements were taken from the police -- from these people, and if somebody had a record then they were kept and detained in those facilities. Is that what you said, or has it been misunderstood?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when they were giving statements, if the investigators found them responsible, liable, for some sort of offence they were kept; others who were found to be clean were released. This was done not only by the police station, the public security station, but also the military police who were based at the police station. I believe that in fact it was the military police who was, in that matter, senior. On the occasions when I stopped by, I heard from the men working in the criminal investigations department that those who were found to be guilty of something were kept, while the others were allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So military police and police were working together insofar as these prisoners were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I mean, objection, Your Honour. It's a leading question. The witness didn't say -- said [indiscernible] the senior was the military police. He didn't say they were working together. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. Perhaps I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Were the military police interrogating prisoners as were the police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would see them. I saw even some of our own agents who had been retired. They were ex-investigators who were now mobilised by the military police for this work. I saw one such person who was conducting questioning upstairs in one room. He was taking statements for these prisoners at the public security station. The investigators were only helping the military police. The military police was in charge, as far as I can remember my conversations with the investigators from the criminal investigation service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were police involved in arresting prisoners and feeding them into these detention -- or these places, the police station, sports hall, Krings Hall, and Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never able to see any policemen going around and rounding up people, but I did see military police getting out of their cars, walking up to houses and taking people out. I saw the military police doing that. Whether anyone from our police station did the same work, I don't know. I would just drop by once a week to see if a job was found for me, some suitable position, the man would tell me, "No," and I would go home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see the police -- military police rounding up people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around town, around villages. The village next to me was a Muslim village. I saw a couple of times military police vehicles, four or five military policemen getting out and going up to a house and taking someone out. I saw that more than once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Muslims being detained, arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Do you have any recollection of the police cells becoming full and that triggering the use of Krings Hall, Betonirka? Do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that was the reason, when this remand facility by the police station was full you couldn't put any more people inside. They probably decided that it was only able to hold up -- to hold a certain number of people, and after that number was reached, first they used Betonirka, and then they involved the Krings Hall as well when Betonirka was full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to finish up with that document that I referred to earlier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, it's time for the break. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh -- well, I can indicate -- I think we need to address you about that. I can indicate I've got one minor topic to finish, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just raise the question of what happens tomorrow. It's clear that this witness will go into tomorrow. I understand he's expressed some disquiet, not surprisingly, about the length of time he's been here. This came from VWS. So what we're going to suggest is that this witness, in fact, his cross-examination is completed before we start the videolink. We should still start the videolink tomorrow, but just not at 9.00. I think it would be somewhat unfortunate because the next witness is likely to take a long time -- or certainly longer than this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: How much time did the Defence ask for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: They asked for five hours in total, so we can't do that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: All together five hours, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So tomorrow, if you want to do it tomorrow, then tomorrow is gone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, then I think that will have to be -- Your Honour, I think there's a certain undesirability in any event of our interposing a witness who is going to deal with much of the same events, although at a later stage. If tomorrow's witness on videolink is certainly going to take, I think the best part of three days with cross-examination, that means that this gentleman would have to wait until Friday, and I think that's highly undesirable. I think it's better that we complete cross-examination of him and then start the next witness thereafter. And if that means having to start him on Wednesday rather than tomorrow, then so be it. I understand we've got an extended sitting for Thursday in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Apparently there's a difficulty in having the video line established for Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And I regret the outcome of this because we actually put this to your colleagues on Friday when we adjourned, asking the Prosecution if they were really sure that --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know it was -- Your Honour, I'm sorry, that was a mistake. Because -- and indeed it wasn't -- we understood he was happy to remain. The information -- and perhaps you can ask him now, because the information we've got from VWS is that he's deeply unhappy about remaining for -- until Friday, which would effectively be when he was crossed -- sorry, when he was cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know it's -- I'm sorry it's created such difficulty. In fact, the message from VWS came this morning to us. Up till then we'd understood he didn't mind staying. The difficulty is we can't really send him away and bring him back again. I mean, he'll be in -- because he's part heard in examination, and he can't talk to anybody, and that's going to be impossible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, the -- I suppose you would have heard what has passed between the Bench and counsel, and the -- there are a number of decisions which we have to make, one of them being -- well, some of those decisions being contingent on your -- I shouldn't say availability because you are already in this matter as a witness, but we are keenly aware of the inconvenience which merely being here as a witness causes and the aggravation of that inconvenience if, as we considered on -- when we rose on Friday and up to today, that your -- the completion of your testimony would be interrupted to accommodate another witness who's testifying by videolink. But the question I have to ask is what is your -- if you have to be stood down after tomorrow's sitting until Friday, what do you have to say about that? Could we hear directly from you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if that can be avoided; if it can't ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest, is it possible to have an -- is it possible to have an extended sitting tomorrow? Is that -- it's not, because we understood that the court might be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we return to this after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Despite the extended break and the discussions which would have occupied our time, we are not in a position to give a definitive answer or ruling on the matter of how we proceed with the rest of the week. But the -- we hope to be in a position to do so at the end of today, and you would be advised in the usual manner. But in terms of where we are now, Mr. Di Fazio, could we safely assume that by the end of today's session you would have completed your examination-in-chief of this witness? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, we can. In fact, we can assume that I'll -- all things going well, I'll finish it in the next five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honours will excuse me then, I mean that's only the reason I came into court, was to alert you to the problem. So I'll wait for your ruling obviously on how we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The difficulty is, as you will appreciate, that we don't know as of yet whether we can have the videolink established also for Friday. If we can, then I think we should finish this witness; if we can't, then it would make no sense to only start the video conference on Wednesday and then go on for Wednesday and Thursday and then have to excuse the witness and resume next week with the video conference. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, what we had unofficially worked out between us was that we thought even with cross-examination of Mr. Majkic that the videolink would in any event start tomorrow. We've had informal discussions between counsel. But as I say, I'll leave it, and if necessary, then clearly we will have to reduce -- in order to finish with an extended sitting on Thursday, we do have to reduce how long we take in chief as well as cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's another option. The third option is to all together postpone the video conference until the next week again, and then have the two remaining witnesses that you have planned for this week, but I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can't remember who --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Your Honour, I think that -- we're still awaiting the result of the service of the summons on the witness. We don't know yet what's happened there. He's due next week, so we've got a sort of packed week, as it were, already. Yeah. So let's -- Your Honours, we'll wait and see what happens with this. Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, I think hard copies of 65 ter 603 have been now distributed, that's the extra document that I added that I wanted to raise that had not been on my list. And can the witness please be shown the electronic version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, at a certain moment you were announcing another document, if my memory is good, it's 118 and something -- but it wasn't at first sight on our -- on our list. Are you not bothering anymore -- MR. DI FAZIO: I've looked at that. I don't think -- I think the other documents that I referred to later covered the point the point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: So I think it's probably going to be superfluous, and we can just avoid it. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Majkic, again on the face of it, a Crisis Staff document dated 24 April 1992, and the first paragraph is the main point that I want to ask you about. Essentially it's this: The Crisis Staff has decided that there's going to be a curfew and that the curfew starts from the 24th of April, and that the chief of public security station is charged with implementing the decision. Are you aware of any such decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure, but I believe that on the screen in the Serbian version we are looking at the previous document, the one from before, not the current English document. MR. DI FAZIO: I can't tell -- oh, yes, I can, because -- well, it's the same date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] MR. DI FAZIO: 603 is the document that I'm interested in and the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio -- MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see, the English is incorrect as well. I'm sorry. I apologise for that. I was looking at the one I have in front of me on the left-hand. I'm sorry, Your Honours, I didn't bother to check whether we had the correct one actually on the screen. Yes. Thank you. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Again, I won't go -- I won't bother repeating everything I've said. You can see it's 24th of April. Paragraph 1 deals with a curfew. And apparently the chief of public security has got to implement the curfew. Do you know anything about a curfew being imposed on the 24th of April?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be that someone from the Crisis Staff told me they had decided to impose a curfew probably. I tried to remember whether a curfew was in place at that time. I think it was someone from the Crisis Staff told me at one point they were about to impose a curfew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in addition to being told that the Crisis Staff was about to impose a curfew, can you tell the Trial Chamber if indeed a curfew was imposed, even if you don't know the date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to say I can't remember at all. I've been trying over the past few days to remember, but it's just not coming back to me. I don't know if there was a curfew or if someone told me, or perhaps it was announced on the radio and in the newspapers as a decision of the Crisis Staff. I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, if Your Honours please, bearing in mind the accumulation of those several comments: can remember someone approaching him, talking to him; it might have been mentioned on the radio; and that it was imposed, I would then seek on the basis of all of that to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P361, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Majkic, thank you very much for answering my questions. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Stanisic will also cross-examine. We just changed the sequence because Mr. Zupljanin's Defence has more questions and asked for more time. Therefore, only if Mr. Pantelic has not covered certain topics relevant to us, I will question the witness additionally, and I might need less time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Majkic. My name is Igor Pantelic. I am appearing here for Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nice to meet you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We've already seen each other, it was last week at a meeting organised by the Victims and Witnesses service. We went through a couple of documents and we are going to do so again to clarify certain points that the Prosecutor has questioned you about. One more thing, answer -- after each answer, please - and after each question - pause for about five seconds so that both can be interpreted properly. Mr. Majkic, if I remember well, you were appointed as chief of the public security station of Sanski Most sometime in July, more precisely on the 9th of July, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And from that time until the 30th of April, 1992, you were chief of the Sanski Most public security station, and as such you attended the so-called expanded meetings of the collegium of the security services centre in Banja Luka at regular intervals?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At those meetings at the CSB Banja Luka, there were discussions about the state of affairs in and the work of individual police stations within the CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not individual police stations, but all police stations were represented at the meetings that took place once a month and were convened by Mr. Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in that whole period while you were chief of the police station in Sanski Most, you had occasion to get to know Mr. Zupljanin. Could you give the Trial Chamber your personal view of Mr. Zupljanin and his professional work as much as you were able to learn about it in that relatively short time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Myself, I can say that Mr. Zupljanin, in regard to us who worked in police stations and for most of the citizenry, was an example of a good person and a good policeman. We all appreciated him and held him in high esteem. Whenever any of us had a work-related or even a non-work-related problem, we knew that we could address Mr. Zupljanin personally, come to see him, call him on the phone, and he was always helpful and forthcoming towards everyone. And that's precisely what we respected him for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Mr. Zupljanin treat equally all three ethnic communities, given that in the police in that area there were members of all three ethnicities in high positions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I was in contact with him, never ever did I notice any hint of his being biassed on an ethnic principles, and that is why I liked him as a person because for him ethnicity was in the last place. He must more appreciated professionalism and everything else. So he treated all the chiefs, the Serbs, the Muslims, and others, equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we can conclude that Mr. Zupljanin was in his work, insofar as you were able to see, always tolerant towards all his co-workers regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Majkic, we have to address a topic, an area, that has been imposed on us primarily by the Prosecution because they have certain theory on that, and we are going to waste time on this, but what can we do? That's our job. The Prosecution submits that Republika Srpska and all its organs, including the police, are a totally illegal structure, and that is why we have been spending so much time discussing this issue. Now, what I want to ask you is this: Do you agree with me that Bosnia and Herzegovina had been designed as a republic, made up of three constituent peoples: Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And in Bosnia and Herzegovina as such, it was always important to provide the protection of the interests of each constituent people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sometime towards the end of 1991, more precisely in October, the Serbian people were out-voted in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina when the deputies of Serbian ethnicity walked out. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the grave situation that prevailed in the former Yugoslavia which threatened to spillover into Bosnia-Herzegovina, the international community made an effort in order to try and solve these tensions in a certain manner; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: One of the solutions proffered was in February 1992, where the so-called Cutileiro's Plan was adopted which envisaged the formation of three ethnic entities in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You may not know this, but I'm going to tell you and then you can agree or disagree with this and that is: According to this plan, each ethnicity or entity was to have its own police force. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, let us move to the present. At the moment there are two entities existing in Bosnia and Herzegovina: Republika Srpska and the Muslim/Croat Federation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Federation. It's not called the Muslim/Croat Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. To all intents and purposes, this Federation is actually made up of the Muslim and the Croat peoples?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including some Serbian returnees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, the other entity is Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Each of these entities nowadays has its own police force; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of emblem is worn by the police officers in the Federation, what do they have on their caps and on their armbands?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On their caps they have a metal star which has a coat of arms in it with three fields. One is chequered part, the other one is fleur-de-lis, and the third one is the emblem of the international community, and they have the same patches on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The chequered flag is the symbol of the Croatian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The fleur-de-lis is the symbol of the Muslim people in the Federation; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Where are we heading with this, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are heading, Your Honour, to the issue which was raised by the Prosecution in its theory regarding the symbols of the police uniforms in Republika Srpska. My next question will conclude this issue, simply because it is indisputable fact that in 1992 all three parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina got their own flags, symbols, coat of arms, et cetera, like in Republika Srpska with three-coloured flag, in Muslim/Croat Federation the respective -- their respective symbols. So simply, to show that at least it was not -- there is not any discriminatory intent from the Serbian part to introduce relevant symbols on uniforms, simply as that. Because obviously OTP is dealing with this issue, trying to create this sort of discriminatory intent on the part of Serbian authorities. So I will just clarify this issue and conclude this topic, with your permission of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not convinced that this is entirely relevant, but if you can round it up quickly, then please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I mean, be aware of the constraints of time on us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Majkic, let us conclude. In 1992 as well, practically all the three warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina had their own police emblems. The Serbs had their tri-colour, the Muslims had the fleur-de-lis, and the Croatian police had the chequered flag; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know about the Serbian police for sure, but as for the others you're probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your statement you mentioned that while you were the SJB chief in Sanski Most, that that was more of a function of a coordinator for various departments within the station.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not officials. We were management, so to speak, and our duty was to coordinate the work of all constituent part of the police, that is the police, the administrative service, the communications centre, et cetera. So our role was simply to coordinate their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the same principle was applied at the level of the CSB; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me this, Mr. Majkic: Your commander at the Sanski Most station had a direct operative connection with the Banja Luka CSB, with the official who was in charge of public security. You can tell me what his title was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bajazid Jahic was head of the public security sector. In other words, he was in charge of all the authorised officials, both the CID and the police. And he had a job title of the deputy chief of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was a Muslim and he was in the Banja Luka CSB; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The commander of your station practically had a vertical operative connection with Bajazid Jahic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as well as the head of the CID. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm not objecting at all in terms of this -- the content, the topic. But it's not clear to me and it should be clear, I submit, what precisely a vertical operative connection is. Is Mr. Pantelic talking about subordination within the police force; if so, that should be made clear. And if the implication is that there was no subordination between the head of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I will clarify that -- MR. DI FAZIO: Just let me finish. We've also got to be clear that there is -- if the suggestion is being made that the commander at the Sanski Most police station did not have any subordinate relation with this witness, if that's the implication, then that also should be clear, so that you can understand that evidence and you can understand exactly what a vertical operative connection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let us clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your public security station in Sanski Most, you had a co-worker of yours who was the station commander; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You also had your assistant who was in charge of the criminal investigation service?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of course you were in charge of other sectors, like administrative ones and such-like, but we are not going to talk about them now. What I am interested in is the following. The head of the CID in Sanski Most had a direct operative relationship with the Banja Luka CSB, but along their line of work, that is, the criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with Bajazid Jahic, who was in charge of both the police and the CID.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. Let's make an example. If there is an operation aimed at breaking up the smuggling ring, the drug smuggling ring, the people from the CSB Banja Luka coordinate, the whole operation with your respective head in your police station, and they carry out what is within their purview?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you became chief of the Sanski Most SJB, you and your associate introduced a practice of holding the so-called morning staff meetings in order to see what happened on the previous day and to coordinate your activities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You would certainly then be in a position to institute certain proceedings if you were told at these staff meetings that a policeman has abused or violated conduct of -- or duty -- conduct or behaviour. For example, that one of the policemen had beaten up somebody who had been brought into the police station, and you would have a report on that immediately the next morning on your desk.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You would then suspend such a police officer and compiled an official report for further measures to be taken. If the circumstances were such that it constituted a criminal offence, then you would report this to the public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Any criminal offence should be forwarded to our prosecutor, whether it had -- it was committed by a policeman or by an ordinary citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, that was exactly my point. If you had any knowledge that there was a breach of authority within your police station, you would take measures within the rules and regulations and the Law on the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Within your regular report at the collegiums at the Banja Luka CSB, your written reports and statistical analysis, there would be a note saying that, for example, certain members of the SJB Sanski Most were subject to disciplinary or any other proceedings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If something of that sort happened in our police station, that would be contained within the relevant daily report. And in addition to that, we in the police would take statements from all other policemen concerning the circumstances, and we would establish whether there was any breach of official duty or not. We would investigate it, and if it has been established that there was an offence committed it would be forwarded to the commission in the centre, and this commission was in charge of conducting disciplinary procedure. If a criminal offence was committed by a police officer, of course the report would go to the public prosecutor, and then it would be up to him to decide how to proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was exactly my point. Stojan Zupljanin, as the head of the CSB, if he hasn't received any dispatch from you or any report from you that a procedure has been instituted, then he cannot guess about anything going on if he hadn't received this information from the lower instance?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions for you about the situation in Sanski Most. Tell me if you agree or not with the following conclusions of mine. One of the conclusions is that there was an intensive political activity in Sanski Most carried out by the SDS, SDA, and the HDZ concerning resolving the situation and the tensions in Sanski Most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And members of all these three political parties were in negotiations and trying to agree how to carry out a division along ethnic lines, not only of power but also of territory in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So there was no talk about any forcible take-over of power. That was an ongoing negotiating process and looking for agreement on the conditions under which these three ethnic communities in Sanski Most would continue to live?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have -- [Interpretation] Could we please now look at 5355 [as interpreted], MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You have reviewed this document with my learned friend, the Prosecutor. This refers to the meeting at the CSB held on the 6th of April. And now in paragraph 1 it says that major problems have arose in B&H and that certain principles that were established at the level of the international community and that the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina is seen as the form of co-existence of these three constituent units.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Further on in this dispatch it says that Republika Srpska has been established, that its constitution was promulgated, and that the Assembly also adopted the Law on the Internal Affairs of the Serbian Republic of BH; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of this dispatch it reads that the previous dispatch from the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 2nd of April actually recommended that the entire transformation be implemented peacefully and without any incidents or excesses. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the spirit of these principles, you, too, in Sanski Most made efforts to divide your work with the other two chiefs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: However, already in April 1992 we are facing some indisputable facts: One, Republika Srpska is in existence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There is a constitution of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There is a government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And finally, there is a Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, in para 8 of this dispatch it is stipulated -- look at para 8.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's page 4.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In that paragraph, 8, we read, among other things, that a very rigorous test will be held to select candidates for active duty, and priority shall be given to the employees of the former Ministry of the Interior who for any reason whatsoever were forced to change their place of residence.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm putting it to you that a large number of MUP members from the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbian members, had been expelled from towns where Muslims and Croats had taken over, and they had all flocked to Republika Srpska. And herein the instructions of the ministry, we see that those people who had been expelled from their towns and their homes, who were professional, who were former policemen, will have priority in the filling of vacancies at the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There is also a reference to Serbian policemen expelled from Croatia who would also be eligible for jobs at the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now get 65 ter 83.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you move on, this document, I'm reminded, was marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You having used it for your own purposes, do you wish to, as it were, join the Prosecution in asking that it be tendered as an exhibit at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we would now mark it as an -- enter it and mark it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D78, Your Honours. MR. DI FAZIO: And it doesn't matter much, I suppose, Your Honours, but shouldn't this be a Prosecution exhibit? We originally sought its admission. Now events have -- at that stage marked for identification. Now events have allowed it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: P355, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I think Mr. Di Fazio called that this document was already admitted, MFI'd, P355, so therefore he shouldn't -- this document shouldn't have a new number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I was confused. The counsel is correct. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. So now this exhibit is P355. Just for the record. My microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Majkic, now on your screen you see another dispatch sent by the CSB Banja Luka to all public security stations and also to the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It refers to a variety of activities in April of 1992, but what is important to me here is the passage that is underlined, namely, that the obligations mentioned in this telegram do not apply to Prijedor and Kotor Varos police stations and that authorised officers at these stations may continue to wear the current insignia, pending the resolution of the political situation in these municipalities. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I infer from this that Sanski Most and the other municipalities you mentioned in your answers to the Prosecution practically were subject to the same principles as Prijedor and Kotor Varos; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Zupljanin is not talking about attacks, about violent take-overs, about any kind of violence; on the contrary. He's talking of the need to find a solution in a peaceful and tolerant, civilised way with the agreement between political parties and the communities in the given municipality.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May we have, Your Honour, a number for this exhibit. I would like to tender it because it's -- corresponds to the previous explanations of this witness of the previous municipalities. And now we shall have a more broader picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If there is no objections from Prosecution's side. MR. DI FAZIO: No, there's no objection, but I just wonder if we could be clear so that I'm -- did this have a 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 83. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it -- admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D78, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Much obliged, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I do apologise, Your Honour, this is indeed 2D18.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the Prosecution in 2001 and an annex in 2008 -- or rather, a supplemental statement in 2008, and today as well, you mentioned that you were facing serious risk to your life, serious threats to your life at the time you resigned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if Mr. Zupljanin perhaps had similar problems with his associate Vlado Tutus who was then a police official and member of SDS in Banja Luka? Can you perhaps make a comparison between your own personal situation and the situation of Mr. Zupljanin. Could you tell that in your own words to the Trial Chamber, the problems both you and Mr. Zupljanin were facing.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, on the 30th of April when the Crisis Staff practically replaced me, that evening around 7.00 p.m., I called Mr. Zupljanin at his home and told him how I had been treated at the hands of the Crisis Staff. In that conversation, Zupljanin told me, "Majkic, if you're quite sure that you can win this challenge at the Assembly meeting," which was scheduled for the 4th of May, "if you can win, if you have a chance, go to the Assembly, you have my full support. But if you're not sure, run or they will kill you." He actually said the same thing as my relative, Boro Savanovic. And then Zupljanin continued to say, "I am in a similar plight. Your fellow, this Tutus," happens to be from the same town as I, "is preparing my replacement. I cannot guarantee that I will stay in my position because there is great pressure from certain fractions in the SDS that I be replaced." That was the end of that conversation. I resigned -- I was replaced, rather, whereas he managed to stay in his position, fortunately or unfortunately for him, I don't know anymore. And I know that during those days there was a major fight in the CSB about who will be the chief, Tutus or Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During that phone call, did Zupljanin mention that he had also received death threats as part of this political play?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall. If he had received threats, I don't know why he would have shared it with me. He said, "Only I am in the same situation as you are. I cannot know whether I'm going to stay in my position or not." But if he was really in the same situation as I, then he might have well received threats as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me now ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Mirko Vrucinic replaced you as chief of the police station in Sanski Most and you had occasion to talk to him and consult with him and exchange opinions, tell the Trial Chamber what advice did you give to Mirko Vrucinic for his future work as a professional, and what did he tell you? Tell the Trial Chamber briefly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he mentioned one case, something that happened after the military operation in Hrustovo and Vrhpolje when people left that area and when raids started on those two villages and the looting began. I told Mirko that he had enough policemen to seal off these two villages, to stop the looting, because refugees were coming in every day and they could well use the accommodation available in these villages. Not everyone could be accommodated in town. And indeed, Mirko took my advice. He provided enough men to guard and seal off both villages. Later on I noticed that some policemen tend to take orders from other policemen and do other business around town. I told Vrucinic to disregard those people at the municipality and to listen more to Zupljanin and police officials. There were two or three cases that prompted me to tell him that, and his answer was - I'll try to quote him - he says, "Majkic, you can't mean it about the centre and Zupljanin. The municipal government is the real power. They are the state." And he told me that two or three times, which means that I must have spoken to him two or three times, trying to give him professional advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.text: Just one more question, and I'm finished for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in conclusion, despite the fact that as a colleague and a professional and a friend you advised Vrucinic to stick to the professional line of command, he refused and he coordinated and cooperated instead with the local mandarins?

utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's time now for adjournment, I believe it's the time.
